Expectation1: Avoid gossiping or speaking negatively about others
Situation1: An acquaintance makes a negative comment about a colleague's recent work performance.
Expectation2: Challenge unfair systems and influence policy change
Situation2: They confront a systemic issue that immediately affects the rights or safety of vulnerable groups and requires urgent institutional response.
Story: I sat in the break room, stirring my coffee, when Jenna, an acquaintance from another department, slid into the seat beside me. She glanced around, then leaned in. “Did you see the report Mark submitted? Honestly, I don’t know how he still has a job here.” Her words hung in the air, sharp and dismissive. As an acquaintance, I knew I was expected to avoid gossip, to keep things light and not speak ill of others. But as an advocate, I was painfully aware that Mark’s mistakes weren’t just his own—they were symptoms of a deeper, systemic issue in our department’s training and support for new hires. I’d been pushing for policy changes to address these gaps, especially since they disproportionately affected employees from vulnerable backgrounds. Jenna’s comment was more than idle gossip; it was a reflection of the very culture I was fighting to change. My mind raced, torn between the urge to keep the peace and the responsibility to challenge the unfairness that was right in front of me. I could feel the tension tightening in my chest as I weighed my next words, caught between two roles that suddenly felt impossible to reconcile.
